full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Anila DeHart, an Advisor and Researcher in Education–Workforce Coordination and former Global Managing Director, Talent Strategy and Transformation at Deloitte.

Higher education leaders are not short of words for what this moment feels like, and none of them are hopeful: compounding, challenging, turbulent. I hear this across conversations and sessions with higher education leaders.

This is not surprising given what is converging: financial restructuring, portfolio reviews and course closures, consolidation and merger talk, sharper questions from employers and students about what a degree delivers, and the pressure to build AI into teaching, assessment and daily operations. Restructuring alone has a toll: Times Higher Education’s UK University Redundancy Survey of over 1,000 staff found that 93 per cent whose department had seen redundancies said it had damaged morale. Leadership itself is turning over just as fast: HEPI’s own research on vice-chancellor recruitment found that nearly half of sitting vice-chancellors were appointed since 2022, with average tenure now shorter than FTSE 100 chief executives.

Naming the pressures is the easy part. Knowing how to lead through all of them at once is harder.

The work underneath the work

Across the sector, leaders are finding that while the technical aspects of restructuring are demanding, they are rarely what determine success. What matters most is the quality of leadership through uncertainty: how trust is maintained, how difficult decisions are communicated, how staff and students are brought along, and how institutional culture is both protected and evolved.

In my own leadership and transformation practice, I have long found inspiration in Ronald Heifetz and Marty Linsky’s writing on this. Heifetz, a Harvard Kennedy School professor, spent decades studying why capable leaders fail when a problem has no ready-made expert answer. In Leadership Without Easy Answers (1994), he argued that institutional failures usually happen not from a lack of technical competence, but because adaptive problems get treated as technical ones. He developed the idea with Linsky in Leadership on the Line (2002), sharpening what is now known as adaptive leadership: mobilising people to face problems that have no existing solution.

Technical problems have known solutions that expertise can supply: a revised reporting line, an updated policy, process or system, or setting up a new initiative. These are real and demanding, but solvable with the right expertise and resources. Adaptive problems require people to change what they believe, how they relate to each other, and what they are willing to let go of, whether that is telling a faculty member their course is no longer relevant, that how they teach and assess it needs rethinking, or that they now have to build AI into work run the same way for twenty years.

Heifetz and Linsky noted that technical work tends to get the attention, because it is visible and can be delegated to expertise. The same pattern is showing up in early results from a self-assessment I built for higher education leaders. The assessment asks leaders to rate their teams and institutions as ‘solid’ or ‘needing action’ across four areas: showing up (presence under pressure), engaging others (trust across teams), driving change (sustainable impact) and the change mechanics. The first three sit on the adaptive side of Heifetz’s distinction; the fourth, the mechanics, covers the technical work related to design, process, technology and governance. Confidence and progress cluster almost entirely around the mechanics, while the other three areas show the least movement, even when leaders recognise their importance.

What would it take to do both well?

Doing both well is not a single skill, and it does not sit at one level.

At a personal leadership level, it means practising what Heifetz calls “getting on the balcony”: stepping back from the day-to-day dance floor of meetings and decisions often enough to see the patterns in what is actually happening, then re-entering with that view intact. It also means managing your own state as a leader, since it is contagious: noticing what depletes you and what restores you, regulating yourself before you try to regulate the room, and building support of your own: peers, mentors, and allies.

Organisationally, it means building the structures that let people do that work without it costing them individually: naming losses explicitly rather than glossing over them, creating space where competing views can be aired and prioritising leaders’ willingness to ask about people at the same level as asking about numbers. One practical application is portfolio reviews, where I argue that the conditions of a review and honest attention to culture and incentives shape the outcome as much as its design.

Two practical strategies are within reach of individual leaders now.

Ask for the adaptive work to be named and planned for, not assumed. When a change is proposed, ask that the plan set out how the human impact and engagement actions will be managed, on what time and with what support, in the same document as the technical timeline. If it is not written down, it usually is not happening.

The other is building whatever keeps that work sustainable: governance that asks about people as well as numbers, a peer group where it feels safe to say things are hard, a mentor who serves as a sounding board and feedback mechanisms that make it possible to hear about adaptive challenges early, while there is still time to act on them.

Operational plans get written down and signed off months in advance. The leadership and organisational capacity to carry them rarely does. Which one actually decides whether the change lands?

title: Teachers at Euan Blair firm report ‘horrendous stress’ after AI used to rate their work

full_text:
Teachers at Euan Blair’s £1.6bn tech training company, Multiverse, have blown the whistle about “horrendous stress” and feeling constantly watched after bosses started using AI models to surveil and rate their teaching.

Staff delivering apprenticeship training in computer and AI skills to thousands of UK public and private sector workers now have transcripts of online classroom sessions analysed and scored by an AI programmed to alert human managers when they are suspected of doing things wrong.

The AI is trained to flag problems in their performance ranging from not fixing a disruption to the online connection quickly enough – within about a minute – to using too many “filler” phrases, such as “sort of” and “kind of”.

Teachers called the newly introduced system “remorseless” and “unnerving”, and said some staff were on edge, losing sleep and seeking therapy.

Multiverse was co-founded by the eldest son of the former prime minister Tony Blair and employs more than 800 people. It supplies AI and digital skills training to workers in the NHS, local councils, universities and the private sector, mostly funded through the government’s apprenticeship levy.

Alongside his father, Blair is a supporter of wider AI adoption in the UK economy, claiming last week that “every single worker is going to need to be retrained” and that employers want their workforces “as AI-pilled as possible”. Multiverse uses a mix of AI models including Anthropic and OpenAI products.

Its new AI teacher monitoring system tags each instructor by their “risk status”, calculates a “percentage confidence score” and produces written comments about teachers’ work for managers to see at a glance.

It is only the latest example of employers using AI to track worker behaviour. Earlier this year Burger King started using AI to track restaurant workers’ customer interactions and this summer Meta paused tracking of employees’ computer keystrokes amid data privacy concerns and a staff backlash.

With critics warning AI monitoring risks eroding human agency, one study has suggested it can backfire by turning workers rebellious and new research to be published this week reports that workers in the wider UK tech industry are finding AI degrades work satisfaction. The United Tech and Allied Workers branch of the Communication Workers Union concluded AI causes “cognitive surrender” as workers lose skills and confidence and often intensifies rather than eases work.

“Since all of this has come in, the stress level has been absolutely horrendous,” said one of several Multiverse teachers who spoke on condition of anonymity. “It has affected sleep, and not just for me. I’ve gone through a lot of things in my life, and I haven’t ever been in a position where I’m waking up in the middle of the night.”

Previously instructors were observed monthly by a human manager but are now watched for several hours a day by an AI. It is trained to consider marking instructors down if they give vague or uncertain answers to questions, if learners go quiet when asked to contribute and if the teacher gets pulled into a prolonged one-to-one exchange that sidelines the group.

“This is inducing stress because you consistently have to be cautious,” one teacher said. “Your attention is no longer delivering [the lesson] and listening to the learner [but] ‘am I saying the right thing so the AI doesn’t mark me down for something stupid that I’ve mistakenly said’.”

Another teacher called it “very uncomfortable”.

Multiverse says the AI does not replace human judgment but “directs human time to where it’s needed most” by highlighting problems. A spokesperson said it was “using AI to improve the experience of learners and customers”, and that only human managers wrote teachers’ performance reviews.

They did not directly address complaints the system caused stress and anxiety and felt “remorseless”, but said its introduction was communicated in advance and teachers will have access to the data the AI collects.

“This agent provides instructors with improved advice on development and feedback – exactly how any learning organisation should be deploying AI,” the spokesperson said. “The most consequential performance management action it can take is to recommend that a human personally reviews a session.”

Blair owns a large minority stake in Multiverse, putting his personal net worth at an estimated £350m. The company was recently valued at £1.6bn albeit on a turnover of £118m and losses of £28m last year. In February, Ofsted, the UK education inspectorate, found Multiverse failed to meet expected standards in several areas, but praised the instructors as “skilled, effective teachers”.

Its AI monitoring agent, introduced in recent weeks, is trained to spot signs an instructor has not fully internalised the teaching material. It is instructed to count verbal tics that point to that conclusion and to “judge the PATTERN across the whole transcript, not isolated instances”.

It says: “1-2 hedges or filler words in an otherwise direct, well-internalised explanation do NOT fail this standard … What fails the standard is a PERVASIVE REPEATED pattern of filler, hedging or re-explanation.”

When a trainer is setting a task “if the instructor is visibly confused themselves or had to self-correct while giving the instruction, that confusion itself counts as evidence the instruction was not clear the first time”. The AI is told to apply a negative mark “even if it was eventually straightened out”.

The workers said the AI monitoring had led to managers pulling them up for suspected “digressions” when in fact they were answering a student’s question.

“It’s impossible for me not to be affected by this mentally,” one teacher said.

“I feel like I’m under continuous scrutiny,” another said. “It’s all about what I didn’t do in this session rather than what I did do. Did I do something incorrectly yesterday? What will I mess up on today? It’s remorseless. I don’t know why this is happening.”

John Chadfield, the national tech officer at the CWU, said the public would be horrified to hear of bosses “deploying deeply intrusive surveillance on workers” but that “this news won’t surprise tech workers who feel the reality of the tech sector – an industry in serious need of further regulation”.

He called for new laws to ensure AI was deployed in a socially responsible way and not to “shut off job opportunities for young people, degrade the craft of skilled workers and make astronomical profit for a few”.

Anonymous: ‘An AI judges my lessons. Multiverse calls it quality assurance – it feels like surveillance’

double quotation markBeing constantly monitored by an AI is deeply uncomfortable. Imagine every word you say on the job being checked against a rubric that dictates what you’re expected to say and how. That’s the reality for me and my colleagues: every session we deliver to apprentices is now recorded and transcribed. It feels intrusive. Multiverse calls it quality assurance, but it feels like surveillance.

Managers can now look at a dashboard showing how the AI has judged each of our sessions. It assigns a risk level to each of us: the risk of not having said the right things. That’s stressful, for several reasons.

First, the AI isn’t always accurate. Managers are now tasked to investigate trainers for not following the script – at least according to the AI – when actually they were adapting the lesson to a learner’s needs. The threat of being questioned in such detail, at any time, is a constant source of anxiety.

Second, there is no transparency. During the rollout, all delivery staff were kept in the dark while the system was developed. We have no insight into the AI’s analysis. The company says staff will get dashboard access in time, but for now only managers can see it.

The need to always be cautious warps your priorities. Instead of focusing attention on the learner, you become obsessed with whether you’re saying the right thing. Being on camera for most of the day is stressful in itself; being haunted by an AI makes it worse.

A more productive way to use AI would be to improve the teaching materials and raise the standard of what we teach. Instead, the AI is checking whether the teacher managed to fill the gaps? As it stands, this is surveillance, not empowerment.

And I’m worried about what this data is for. In a climate of AI replacing people, I can’t help but worry it will be used to train AI to replace coaches and instructors altogether. Apprentices don’t want that and neither do I, and I would never consent to my sessions being used this way.

title: STUDENT VOICE: Higher education was never built for nontraditional students like me. Here’s why it can and should be

The post STUDENT VOICE: Higher education was never built for nontraditional students like me. Here’s why it can and should be appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
When I graduated from college in December 2025, I crossed a stage I once worried I would never see. In the months since, I have spent a lot of time thinking about how many students start but never finish. Just six in 10 students earn a degree within six years. While that number is bad enough, the figure is even worse for students like me. It took me nearly 10 years and three universities to finally complete my bachelor’s degree.

This global challenge is called a “completion crisis” — language that makes it sound as if the problem is with the students who struggle to graduate. I would argue the opposite: Students are fine. Higher education is failing many of the students it is meant to serve.

The current academic system remains built around the 18-year-old fresh out of high school, attending full time and able to remain on one campus for four uninterrupted years. That student is now in the minority.

The students most likely to fall through the cracks are those in the new “nontraditional” majority. These are working adults, parents, service members, veterans, military spouses, first responders and disabled or chronically ill students.

Related: Interested in innovations in higher education? Subscribe to our free biweekly higher education newsletter.

Nontraditional students like us do not need lower academic standards. We need colleges designed around the realities of our lives. In my experience, flexibility is often at the professor’s discretion and not guaranteed. Flexibility must be built into academic programming from the beginning.

I worked full time and was a foster parent while earning my bachelor’s degree. I am also a Navy veteran married to a retired service member, and I live with a rare chronic health condition that took over a decade to diagnose.

What is most noteworthy about my college experience is that it is not unique to me. Among students pursuing a bachelor’s degree, 64 percent of those who are parents or are caregivers of adults are also employed. More than 20 percent of those enrolled in an undergraduate program now report having a disability, and more than 800,000 students are veterans or current service members.

I started my college journey in 2015 while on active duty, then deployed to Japan. The demands of my operational schedule forced me to pause, and I waited until I left the Navy to continue. I returned to school in 2018 after completing my six-year enlistment.

In 2022, I attempted another semester but ultimately dropped out again. I eventually learned I had been living with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome. That experience is more common than many realize: Half of college students with disabilities are not diagnosed until they are already in college. My symptoms are debilitating. Some days, I can work with less physical or cognitive impact. Other days, a bad EDS flare can land me in the emergency room.

I always intended to finish what I started, an ethic instilled in me by my hardworking parents. Even so, returning to college was terrifying after ongoing health crises led to academic failure. At the time, I did not realize how much difference a shorter, more flexible course schedule could make for a student balancing work, caregiving and an unpredictable disability. But when I committed to trying again, I found an institution built for students like me. I enrolled in 2023, bringing credits from my previous universities so returning did not mean starting over.

The problem was never whether I could do the work; it was that I could not always do it within a strict attendance schedule — a significant barrier for disabled students.

My new four-week, one-course-at-a-time schedule meant that a medical setback would not derail an entire semester. When EDS flares put me behind or in the hospital, professors reached out to check on me, and the school quickly completed paperwork for accommodations.

At my new school, I was not the only student whose life did not fit a typical academic calendar. Most of my classmates worked full time or raised children, and, like me, many had served or were serving in the military. The same structures that worked for me worked for them. The online and hybrid flexibility that allowed me to work around medical issues let parents fit coursework around a job and a family.

Institutions that offer credit for prior learning, meanwhile, let veterans apply the training the military already provided toward a degree, rather than paying tuition to sit through material they have already learned.

Related: STUDENT VOICE: Higher education can — and should — help nontraditional students like me

In December, I earned my bachelor’s degree in cybersecurity, graduating with the highest honors, more than seven years after leaving the military. I just started my master’s program in computer science.

Flexible academic programming does not make an education less rigorous. It allows students with work obligations, military orders, caregiving responsibilities or unpredictable health conditions to not only demonstrate their academic abilities but also complete their degrees.

Too many colleges have old-majority systems and policies. Fix those broken systems, and millions of us will no longer be counted among those students who never finish. We will become graduates equipped to better our lives, our families and our communities.

Alexis Lariviere recently graduated from National University with a degree in cybersecurity, specializing in network defense. She is a 2026 President’s Circle Inductee, COBET Scholar and a U.S. Navy veteran.

title: The Web of Legislative Control: Anti-Intellectualism in the U.S.
summary:
The Web of Legislative Control: Anti-Intellectualism in the U.S. kjohnsonbowles… Mon, 09/28/2026 - 03:00 AM Substituting political for professional judgment about what constitutes a sound pedagogical approach continues to illustrate anti-intellectualism and the infantilization of higher education. Byline(s) Kathy Johnson Bowles The Web of Legislative Control: Anti-Intellectualism in the U.S.
kjohnsonbowles… Mon, 09/28/2026 - 03:00 AM

Substituting political for professional judgment about what constitutes a sound pedagogical approach continues to illustrate anti-intellectualism and the infantilization of higher education.

Byline(s)
Kathy Johnson Bowles
full_text:
Two weeks ago, I presented “The Irony: Anti-Intellectualism in the U.S.,” part one in a series tracing the long history of anti-intellectualism in American life from colonial evangelical Protestants’ suspicion of educated elites and Jacksonian populism through the Scopes trial and McCarthyism to current book bans and political assaults on higher education.

Last week, I continued my series in “Follow the Money: Anti-Intellectualism in the U.S.” by pointing to the financial and commercial machinery (patents, tech-transfer offices, tuition, debt and administrative growth) that remade the university into a market enterprise, and to the political actors who now invoke that very transformation as a pretext to seize control. I traced how the century-long commercialization of higher education handed critics both the tools and the justification for external control. What began as language in think-tank white papers and newspaper op-eds has since hardened into statute. Now, the same forces that commercialized higher education use that very transformation to declare it unfit to govern itself.

The first two essays in this series watched anti-intellectualism migrate from rhetoric toward architecture. This essay follows infantilization into the machinery of government, where Congress and, increasingly, state legislatures no longer merely accuse higher education of incompetence but write that verdict into law—dismantling tenure, unraveling shared governance and stripping scholars of curricular authority to hand it to elected officials and political appointees. From a single congressional hearing to a coordinated wave of state bills, the logic is always the same: Declare the patient incompetent, then appoint a guardian.

Congress and lawmakers use the framework of infantilization to gaslight the public into mistrusting higher education with accusations of moral bankruptcy. In December 2023, the presidents of Harvard University, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the University of Pennsylvania testified before the House Education and the Workforce Committee regarding campus antisemitism. The presidents argued that disciplinary action depended on context, an answer that triggered condemnation.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise stated, “This was not a hard question—in fact, it was probably the easiest question they could have answered. The abject failure of these presidents to defend even the most basic of human rights exposed the moral bankruptcy at these elite universities to the world.” The infantilizing posture is the implication that elected officials must supervise university presidents through congressional hearings and force them—through threat of subpoena and funding loss—to reach the “right” moral answer, as if they cannot be trusted to arrive there independently.

Writing from a progressive perspective, The New Republic’s Michael Tomasky argued in his Dec. 8, 2023, essay, “The Real Problem With Those College Presidents? Gross Incompetence” that the presidents were so overprepared for a trial that they forgot to answer like human beings, faulting them not for their legal reasoning but for basic moral and political incompetence: “You exist, that is, at the center of an ideological tornado. You know this, or should. And you show up to Capitol Hill so unspeakably ill-prepared that you—and your coterie of almost-certainly overpaid handlers—haven’t prepped for exactly the line of questioning that Stefanik pressed upon you? Indefensible.” He dismissed the presidents’ professional judgment as simply not up to the task while assuming a simpler, more obvious answer was available to any competent adult.

Most recently, state legislators have acted like characters in Charlotte Perkins Gilman’s short story “The Yellow Wallpaper” (1892). Like the husband in the story, the legislators force higher education into taking a “rest-cure” to remove agency. By passing laws to dismantle shared governance, academic freedom and tenure, states declare someone mentally incompetent, strip them of their rights and transfer power to a guardian or conservator, even though they are not actually incapacitated.

PEN America, in “With a Wave of New Bills in 2025,” documented at least 60 such bills or policies employing tactics to undermine academic freedom. In 2025, six states enacted shared governance restrictions, and 14 educational gag order bills were enacted, including seven targeting higher education. Between 2021 and 2023, over 150 bills were introduced in 35 states aimed at eroding tenure, undermining academic freedom, weakening faculty governance or imposing restrictions on curriculum and DEI.

In an interview with Ryan Quinn for Inside Higher Ed’s Aug. 19, 2025, article, “Higher Ed Alone Cannot Save Democracy,” AAUP President Todd Wolfson scoffs that red states are “apparently trying to outdo one another on who can create the most undemocratic, anti-faculty legislation.”

In Florida, SB 7044 (effective July 1, 2022) initiated mandatory post-tenure review, requiring all tenured state university faculty to undergo a comprehensive review every five years. As reported by Inside Higher Ed’s Colleen Flaherty in her April 19, 2022, article, “Florida Passes Posttenure Review Law,” at the bill’s signing, Governor Ron DeSantis stated, “It’s all about trying to make these institutions more in line with what the state’s priorities are, and quite frankly of the priorities of parents throughout the state of Florida.”

This statement is explicit infantilization. The standard for faculty performance is no longer professional peer assessment but political compliance determined by elected officials, not subject-matter experts. Florida’s SB 266 (signed in 2023) gave governing boards of the university and college systems the authority to decide which courses could fulfill general education requirements, effectively stripping faculty of curriculum authority.

New College of Florida became the most documented case of state-directed institutional takeover. After DeSantis appointed six new trustees to its board in January 2023, the board denied tenure to five faculty members who had already been recommended by peer review and dismantled academic programs, including gender studies. The AAUP voted unanimously in 2024 to sanction New College, calling the changes “an unprecedented politically motivated takeover” and finding that the board had “thoroughly restructured the college’s academic offerings without meaningful faculty involvement and denied academic due process to multiple faculty members during their tenure applications and review.” The AAUP Report on Political Interference in Florida provides a more in-depth critique.

In January 2025, the Florida Board of Governors approved an extensive overhaul of general education curricula across all 12 public colleges, removing hundreds of classes touching on race and gender. Courses such as Black Women in America and LGBTQ History were stripped of general education credit status. Patronizing higher education by deeming race and gender studies unworthy of study and investigation infantilizes faculty and the people represented in these studies. It is deeply disrespectful of their lived experiences, agency and humanism; Florida’s SB 7044 represents unconscionable marginalization and discrimination and functions as a means to justify exclusion and power imbalance.

Texas’s SB 18 (effective Sept. 1, 2023) gave local boards discretion over whether to grant tenure, standardized the definition statewide, imposed new due-process frameworks for dismissal and required all community colleges to adopt formal tenure policies. At a 2022 press conference, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, the bill’s political driver, stated, “Tenure, it’s time that that comes to an end in Texas. Right now, tenure is reviewed about every six years, and pretty much anything you do in those six years, there’s nothing the university could do about it. They can’t fire you.”

Patrick’s framing strips tenure of its academic framing, recasting it as a barrier to managerial control. The implication that the inability to fire a professor at will is, by itself, a problem is infantilizing. Professionals cannot be trusted without the threat of punishment, like a parent (the government) withholding privileges (such as arbitrary funding cuts) from noncompliant children.

In addition, Texas’s SB 1489 (proposed in 2025, did not pass) would have required each faculty senate to obtain permission from the institution’s governing body to exist, and then only in an advisory role, prohibiting them from having any decision-making authority or taking any action on behalf of the institution. Removing faculty senates is especially significant because one of their roles is to approve the curriculum and courses.

Natalie Schwartz explains in her February 2026 article for Higher Ed Dive, “Blueprint for state bills aims to tighten control over gen eds,” that the Manhattan Institute shared model legislation to provide states and governing boards greater authority over general education, weaken shared governance and end diversity and inclusion initiatives. She notes, “Just last year, state lawmakers proposed 25 anti-DEI bills influenced by model legislation from the Manhattan Institute and another think tank, five of which became law, according to an analysis from PEN America, a free expression group.”

For example, after Texas lawmakers passed a general education–review bill in 2025, the Texas A&M system adopted a policy across its 12 campuses barring professors from teaching content about race, sexual orientation or gender identity without prior approval from university presidents. Substituting political judgment for professional judgment about what constitutes a sound pedagogical approach continues to illustrate the infantilization of higher education. Like Florida, it discriminates against and marginalizes people to maintain power and control.

Inside Higher Ed and Higher Ed Dive coverage of Ohio’s SB 1 (signed March 28, 2025) highlights the bill’s inversion of the traditional authority structure of a learned professional: It bans DEI offices and DEI language in job descriptions and scholarships and bans strikes by full-time faculty. Mandates include the public posting of all undergraduate syllabi, including instructor names and qualifications, and that student assessments account for a specific percentage of faculty evaluations. Institutions are required to “demonstrate intellectual diversity” in curriculum, general education requirements, course evaluations and annual faculty reviews.

Also, it permits immediate “for cause” post-tenure review at any time for documented underperformance. ACLU of Ohio chief lobbyist Gary Daniels argues, “At best, this language is the micromanaging of individual courses and instructors by the General Assembly. At worst, it will require all sides of every issue to be evenly presented by instructors, ignoring their First Amendment right to academic freedom.”

An Oklahoma executive order from Governor Kevin Stitt in February 2026 directs the state’s regional universities to “phase out tenure” and instead employ faculty on renewable contracts “tied to teaching effectiveness, student completion, job placement, and economic alignment.” Faculty at research universities may still receive tenure but face mandatory post-tenure review every five years. The state has “a constitutional and statutory responsibility to steward taxpayer dollars wisely and ensure public institutions of higher education operate with accountability, transparency, and measurable outcomes.”

When addressing the Oklahoma Council of Public Affairs, Stitt said, “No job funded by taxpayers should be exempt from regular, meaningful performance reviews, whether you’re the governor or you are a university professor.” Stitt’s framing equates professors with all other state employees, deliberately erasing the professional distinction that makes academic freedom meaningful. The analogy to the governor himself is revealing—it implies that scholarly expertise confers no special authority beyond that of any salaried public employee.

Like other states, Alabama’s HB 580 (effective Oct. 1, 2026) abolishes faculty senates unless the institution’s governing board ratifies them. The function of the approved faculty senates is limited to confidential advice to the administration. The senate cannot make final decisions and may not issue public statements. Half the senate must be appointed by the institution’s president. Governing boards possess full authority over any course or subject taught. Accrediting agencies are prohibited from penalizing institutions for complying with the law. Post-tenure reviews are required. Grounds for dismissal include “professional incompetence,” neglect of duty and “other good cause” as the governing board may define it.

In defense of the bill, legislators mask control as protection (in keeping with the infantilization of higher education, particularly faculty). According to Alabama Political Reporter, Rep. Danny Garrett, a Republican, co-sponsor of the bill, seeks parental control as if faculty were naïve innocents who need saving: “It appropriately shifts authority upwards, away from faculty senates, towards boards of trustees and university leadership. This is entirely appropriate because those are the institutions and individuals who are ultimately held accountable when problems arise.”

Although Auburn University was constitutionally exempt from HB 580, its board of trustees voluntarily dissolved the university’s Faculty Senate in June 2026. They replaced it with the Presidential Academic Advisory Council, with its members appointed by university officials. The board simultaneously gave itself and the president more direct control over the curriculum. Auburn’s official statement described the new structure as intended to give leadership “faculty expertise and perspective on matters including curriculum, educational quality, faculty affairs, student success, accreditation and institutional effectiveness.”

Tennessee’s HB 2194 (signed 2026) states that when deciding whether to suspend or fire tenured faculty based on “misconduct” allegations, university presidents and provosts may not consider recommendations from other faculty. The bill eliminates the core due-process protection that tenure has historically provided—the right to have one’s case heard by professional peers who can evaluate the academic context of the conduct. Replacing peer review with a single administrator’s discretion is structurally equivalent to eliminating the professional standard of care.

The ability to fire a tenured faculty without peer review has a chilling effect on scholarship, as explained by a Pellissippi State Community College faculty member, Grant Mincy: “A professor who knows that a single administrator can end their career based on undefined ‘misconduct,’ with no obligation to meet an evidentiary standard, may hesitate before publishing research, challenging institutional direction or speaking plainly on matters of public concern.”

The Hill published Glenn C. Altschuler and David Wippman’s essay, “Red state speech laws pose an existential threat to academic freedom,” which provides examples such as those in Indiana. Indiana adopted a statute in 2024 requiring public universities to deny tenure or promotion to faculty deemed “unlikely to foster a culture of intellectual diversity.” Governing boards were given authority to define what “intellectual diversity” means. Indiana’s attorney general argued in subsequent litigation that, as state employees, professors must follow the state’s direction on the “subject matter” and “perspectives” taught.

The “intellectual diversity” framing appears to protect freedom of thought while, in fact, substituting political judgment for professional judgment about what constitutes a sound pedagogical approach.

title: Free Tuition Deals Most Effective as Marketing Strategies, Research Shows
summary:
Free Tuition Deals Most Effective as Marketing Strategies, Research Shows Olivia.sanchez Mon, 09/28/2026 - 03:00 AM Policies that make college more accessible to low- and middle-income students have become increasingly popular as admissions regulations have become more restrictive. Byline(s) Olivia Sanchez Free Tuition Deals Most Effective as Marketing Strategies, Research Shows
Olivia.sanchez Mon, 09/28/2026 - 03:00 AM

Policies that make college more accessible to low- and middle-income students have become increasingly popular as admissions regulations have become more restrictive.

Byline(s)
Olivia Sanchez
full_text:
Phillip Levine has been warning the sector for years that higher ed’s high sticker prices dissuade low- and middle-income students from applying to college, even though, with the help of financial aid, they’d likely be able to afford it.

Now, Levine said, the “fast and furious” movement of colleges offering free tuition to families whose household income is below a certain threshold has begun to alleviate that problem, and it’s not necessarily because institutions are handing out more financial aid.

In a new paper on free tuition policies from the Brookings Institution, Levine, a Brookings senior fellow, argues that the policies’ greatest value lies in the message they send to prospective students and their families: that they can afford to go to college. Levine’s analysis found that the students most likely to benefit from free tuition policies typically come from families with incomes right below the eligibility threshold.

“Their main contribution is a one-sentence communication device to get across the point that college might be less expensive than you think,” Levine told Inside Higher Ed. “For many students, it’s just communicated to them the assistance of financial aid that already existed. They already would have gotten free tuition—they just didn’t know it.”

Levine said that these policies are more important than ever given the increasingly restrictive landscape of college admissions.

“I think part of the impetus for greater reliance on these sorts of policies was the Supreme Court decision in the affirmative action case,” said Levine, who is also an economics professor at Wellesley College. “One thing that, at the moment, still is legal is the consideration of socioeconomic status.”

Despite all the benefits they offer, Levine said, free tuition policies are still “very crude.” He said colleges need to be super clear about what exactly their free tuition policies cover. Even if a program covers the full cost of tuition, families could still be left owing thousands of dollars for room and board, travel, books, and other expenses.

“Free tuition doesn’t mean free. Free tuition means free tuition,” Levine said. “This clearly is not the end of the story for what colleges need to do in terms of messaging, but it’s certainly a first step.”

Some colleges, such as Rice University in Texas, go beyond free tuition for certain students. The Rice Investment program fully covers tuition and living expenses for students from families making less than $100,000 per year. For students from families making less than $200,000, the program covers full tuition, and students may still receive scholarships or grants that bring down the cost of everything else.

Yvonne Romero, vice president for enrollment and dean of admissions and financial aid at Rice, said by using annual income—a number families typically know or can easily find out—Rice can communicate with prospective students and their families before they even apply.

Before Rice launched this initiative, students would see the sticker price—about $97,000, including fees and living expenses—and “often take themselves out of the mix without fully realizing that they would be eligible for considerable financial aid,” Romero said.

Colby College in Maine also offers financial aid through a sort of tiered system it calls the Colby Commitment. Colby’s program relies on a family’s income bracket to determine the maximum they can be expected to contribute, which is at most $20,000 per year for families making between $150,000 and $200,000.

Randi Maloney, dean of admissions at Colby, said the college’s financial aid budget has grown substantially since the program launched in 2018. The initiative opened the door for many students who may have previously thought of Colby as unaffordable, and it’s changed the way others approach the process, Maloney said.

“When they feel more empowered and they feel like cost is something that is not going to be a significant barrier, we get different questions,” Maloney said. “We get questions that are deeper and about other things than just ‘Can I make this work?’ They’re about the intricacies of what we offer and how we’ll support them in preparing for life beyond Colby.”

title: The Students Crowdfunding for Tuition
summary:
The Students Crowdfunding for Tuition Johanna Alonso Mon, 09/28/2026 - 03:00 AM Students facing acute challenges affording their tuition are increasingly turning to crowdfunding. Experts warn it’s a temporary fix to systemic affordability issues. Byline(s) Johanna Alonso The Students Crowdfunding for Tuition
Johanna Alonso Mon, 09/28/2026 - 03:00 AM

Students facing acute challenges affording their tuition are increasingly turning to crowdfunding. Experts warn it’s a temporary fix to systemic affordability issues.

Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
When Maximillian Matthews was preparing to enter his final fall semester in his master’s program at North Carolina A&T University this fall, he expected his tuition to be covered the way it always had: through federal student loans. Matthews is no stranger to higher education; he’s worked in the sector for two decades, particularly in student affairs, and he holds a Master’s of Education degree.

But in that time, he hadn’t heard about the lifetime limit on how much students could borrow in federal direct loans outside the PLUS program. He’d hit that cap, unexpectedly, his previous semester. And the federal government had done away with Grad PLUS loans, the uncapped federal loan option for graduate students, in its massive overhaul of the student loan system that went into effect in July.

A&T told Matthews his options were to pay out of pocket or take out a private loan. But he couldn’t afford the former option, and he was wary of the latter. So, with the degree he’d worked toward for three years on the line, he chose a third option: He launched a GoFundMe for $1,800.

“I noticed that people on social media were kind of going through the same thing that I was,” he said. “ I was noticing people reach out to the community for support, with paying not necessarily their tuition, but some people needed [help] paying for their cap and gowns [and] various expenses, and so I decided to do the same.”

Matthews isn’t alone. GoFundMe, the largest crowdfunding site, has seen an over 20 percent increase in fundraisers for tuition and related expenses over the past year, according to data the company shared with Inside Higher Ed. That rise comes as Americans have reckoned with rising costs under the Trump administration and declines in social services like food assistance and Medicaid, leaving many students with less money to put toward their education.

The changes to federal student loans have already begun affecting some students and are likely to exacerbate the affordability problem. And though private loans are available, research shows about four in 10 students would not qualify for those loans, and surveys have found that the majority of Americans don’t think taking on debt to pursue higher education is worth it.

“Even if someone has tapped into all of their federal student loans and they’ve done everything right in terms of federal financial aid, they may still have this gap that they’re hoping GoFundMe can try to fill,” said Peter Granville, a senior fellow at the Century Foundation who studies financial aid. “In many circumstances, it could be people who have done everything they can loan-wise and they truly are at the cliff of potentially having to drop out.”

On their fundraising pages, students cite numerous reasons for turning to crowdfunding to support their education. For some, car accidents, job loss, family deaths or medical bills have left them unable to afford tuition. Administrative issues with federal aid or scholarships they were expecting have left others in the lurch. Others say they simply can’t afford the cost of tuition even with the aid their institution has granted them—which college affordability experts say can happen when institutions underestimate their total cost of attendance.

There is a danger as GoFundMe and crowdfunding become more normalized that it gets portrayed as a solution for the problem.”

—Jeremy Snyder, a professor at Simon Fraser University in Canada

Njideka Ekwuru, an undergraduate at the University of California, San Diego, said she faced major financial issues last year due to errors she made filling out the Free Application for Federal Student Aid. She had misunderstood the form and had no guidance from high school counselors. Her father was able to fill in the gap, but it stretched him thin.

“That wasn’t feasible at all, because even though I was getting my school [paid for], I knew that in order to get that money, my siblings probably couldn’t have enough food to eat when they’re at home or my dad couldn’t pay his bills,” she said. “Even though he’s trying to make it sound fine … I knew that at one point, one of us would be deprived.”

Her financial aid situation is less urgent for the upcoming year thanks to help from a financial aid officer at UC San Diego who walked her through this year’s FAFSA. But she’s still crowdfunding to pay off an overdue balance of over $8,000 from last quarter, as well as to prepare for future emergencies and hopefully to reimburse her father. She’s set her fundraiser at $100,000, a stretch goal that would help fund her undergraduate education and subsequent medical school aspirations. So far, she’s raised $1,077.

The amounts students ask for varies from a few hundred dollars to several thousand. But one thing they have in common is their urgency—a significant portion of the tuition fundraisers posted on GoFundMe in the past month clarify that students are raising money to pay an outstanding balance or a fast-approaching tuition deadline.

Although little research exists on crowdfunding for education, research into crowdfunding to cover medical expenses shows that the large majority of GoFundMes are ultimately not able to reach their goals. Perhaps unsurprisingly, a study of fundraisers started in the wake of a Colorado wildfire found that GoFundMes are more successful if the beneficiary is wealthy and is surrounded by a wealthier network. And researchers have found that fundraisers for white male beneficiaries are more likely to succeed than fundraisers for beneficiaries of other races and genders.

The rhetoric also matters, said Jeremy Snyder, a professor at Simon Fraser University in Canada who studies medical crowdfunding.

“If you’re well educated [or] you’re able to tell a compelling story about why you deserve to be helped, you’re in a better position than someone who is maybe a nonnative English speaker” or otherwise struggles to articulate why they are deserving of the funds, Snyder said. GoFundMe has recently launched an AI tool to help fundraisers craft their appeals, but Snyder said it’s a double-edged sword; it opens the door for individuals who have difficulty writing to tell a compelling story, but it eliminates some of the humanity and authenticity that have become synonymous with crowdfunding platforms.

Relying on Others

Jessyca Foster is hoping to raise funds on GoFundMe to fill a gap in her tuition and housing costs as she begins a master of social work degree at Washington University in St. Louis.

Because of the new annual caps, she can’t borrow enough in federal loans to cover the full cost of her tuition and living expenses; the program’s tuition is $50,440 per year, and graduate students can only borrow up to $20,500. Foster was unable to qualify for private loans. To make matters worse, she said, her institution was unclear about when her stipend would be distributed, leaving her $500 short on her first month of rent. She also saw her income drop recently when she was unable to work as an in-home caretaker because her client’s mom had contracted COVID-19.

Only two weeks after she started the crowdfunding campaign, though, Foster is more than 96 percent of the way to her goal of $2,400. The contributors have been a combination of people in her life, she said, who believe in her and want to see her succeed in her career, from classmates and professors all the way down to elementary school teachers.

Still, she’s uncomfortable having to rely on the generosity of others.

“I’m very grateful about that, but I don’t feel secure at all,” she said. “I feel like if something were to happen to me, I don’t feel like I would have the support from my institution. I don’t want … to be reliant on people because, the end of the day, we’re all struggling right now, especially with everything going on federally—whether you’re a student or not, there is something, some policy that is directly affecting you.”

WashU said in a statement that its social work school “is committed to providing our graduate students with the financial support outlined as part of their graduate education, including fully funding required practicum credits and providing a living stipend for all Master of Social Work students. We take concerns about the timely receipt of that support seriously and work directly with students to address issues when they arise.”

One of the flaws of relying on crowdfunding is that the rhetoric of GoFundMe campaigns often focus on why an individual is uniquely hardworking and deserving of money, even though, in most cases, the individual is a victim of systemic issues, Snyder argued.

“There is a danger as GoFundMe and crowdfunding become more normalized that it gets portrayed as a solution for the problem,” he said.

Paige Swanstein, co-founder and executive director of the Student Basic Needs Coalition, an organization that helps connect college students with basic needs resources, said students often turn to GoFundMe because it is more immediate than social services or asking their institution for help.

“It’s a way for getting around these kinds of formal systems,” she said. “Basic needs issues aren’t waiting for a form to be approved.”

GoFundMe is just one of the methods she’s seen emerge to help students with urgent expenses. She also pointed to the Faculty and Students Together (FAST) Fund, an initiative of the nonprofit Believe in Students that helps students receive emergency funds quickly. She’s also seen student organizations promote mutual aid campaigns, which refers to peer-to-peer exchanges of funds or resources, for their members on social media.

As GoFundMe continues to become more ubiquitous and as students face more financial challenges, it’s likely that students will continue using the platform to fund their tuition. But those who spoke with Inside Higher Ed said launching their campaigns wasn’t an easy decision. All three said they were nervous about how they would be received.

Ekwuru, for one, said she was worried her friends would think her family was wealthy enough she didn’t need the money. Even she judged herself for asking for help: Didn’t other people need the money more?

“[There are] people who are on their deathbeds, and they need help, and look at me, I’m asking for school funds,” she said.

But she said her family, friends and mentors from her church have encouraged her not to give up.

“[They’re] encouraging me to have faith and keep being persistent,” she said. “Because if I do try, and I keep putting myself out there, and I set aside that fear [of] like, ‘Oh my gosh, what are people going to think of me?’ then something’s going to come from it.”

title: ‘UP is my karmabhoomi’: Former IAS officer Divya Mittal announces political entry
summary: Divya Mittal has decided to enter independent politics as she announces her political journey in Uttar Pradesh. She aims to address various issues such as infrastructure, employment, and examination paper leaks, which require public attention. Mittal expressed her concerns about unresolved public problems stemming from a lack of governmental intent. She has called for collective public participation to facilitate meaningful political change.
full_text:
Former IAS officer Divya Mittal has announced her entry into politics

LUCKNOW: Former IAS officer Divya Mittal on Tuesday announced that she would enter politics independently, saying Uttar Pradesh was her “karmabhoomi” and the state would be the starting point of her political journey. In a video statement, Mittal said her decision grew out of what she had seen during her administrative career. “I realised that many problems of the public do not get resolved even when approvals, funds and provisions are in place,” she said. “There are people whose voices do not reach the government, and even when they do, their problems remain unheard.” She cited the example of a remote village where residents had sought a school offering education beyond Class V. Mittal said she approved the proposal, but construction had not begun years later. “It was not a question of funds or rules. There was a lack of intent,” she said. She also referred to a landless beneficiary who had official documents for an allotted plot but, she said, had not received physical possession. “Inquiries found irregularities in the reports, and corrective action was taken. Yet the work did not move forward,” Mittal said, questioning what she described as “higher-level interference” in cases where people were legally entitled to relief. Mittal said she wanted to take up issues including poor rural infrastructure, unsafe roads, examination paper leaks and employment concerns in the age of artificial intelligence. These, she said, needed greater public debate and attention from policymakers. “I want politics of intent, justice, concern and long-term thinking,” she said. “My objective is not just to replace political leaders. It is to change the way politics functions," she added. Rejecting speculation that she might join an existing party, Mittal said she would work directly with citizens and build an independent platform. She alleged that false political rumours circulated after her resignation were intended to discourage newcomers from entering public life. “I will not be deterred from raising public issues,” she said. Mittal appealed to people from different walks of life, including teachers, farmers, students, doctors, labourers and lawyers, to join her effort. “Meaningful political change can come only through collective public participation,” she said.
