title: PMO reviews Ambedkarite writings in university curricula after anonymous post calls them ‘poison’
summary: Academic Kancha Ilaiah Shepherd questions the interference of the PMO in the syllabus of universities, which ought to be in the purview of the Department of Higher Education or University Grants Commission
full_text:
Works of prominent intellectuals and academics recommended as readings in several higher learning institutions are under the scanner of the Higher Education Department, following an enquiry by the Prime Minister’s Office, which was triggered by an anonymous social media post terming these works ‘poison’. The authors/editors of the works include B.R.Ambedkar, Jyoti Rao Phule, Gail Omvedt, Braj Ranjan Mani, and Sharmila Rege, among others.

An urgent online missive from the department to all the central universities on Sunday (September 27, 2026) referred to communication received from the PMO regarding the post and sought their ‘comments’. Further, the email sought details about enrolment in the courses mentioned in the post.

“All the Central Universities are requested to furnish comments on the above. Further, enrollment in the courses mentioned in the tweet may also be apprised to the Ministry [sic],” the communique said, before marking the matter as ‘Urgent’, and seeking the comments/information ‘at the earliest’.

The post/tweet was shared on the platform X on September 26, 2026. It read:“THIS IS WHAT STUDENTS ARE BEING TAUGHT AT OUR UNIVERSITIES

From patriarchy to Caste Annihilation to Debrahmanising the history to Curse of Manu we are feeding young minds with a poison which our leftist cabal use a apprenticeship for grooming their future rank and file [sic]” the post said, looping in a thread of six more posts on the subject.

Attached to the post was an image with a list of 35 works-- notably even Ramayana and Mahabharata-- while the extended thread singled out the works: Annihilation of Caste by B.R. Ambedkar, Against the Madness of Manu: B.R. Ambedkar’s writings on Brahminical Patriarchy’ compiled by Sharmila Rege, ‘Ghulamgiri’ by Jyotirao Phule, ‘Debrahmanising History: Dominance and Resistance in Indian Society’ by Braj Ranjan Mani, ‘Dalits and Democratic Revolution’ and ‘Towards a Historical Materialist Analysis of the Origins and Development of Caste’ both by Gail Omvedt, ‘Mahishasur, Ek Jananayak’ and ‘Mahishasur: Mithak aur Paramparayen’ by Pramod Ranjan, ‘Bharat Ke Moolnivasi aur Arya-Akraman’ by Swapan Kumar Biswas, ‘Bharat Ke Moolnivasi: Rigvedic Asur aur Sharanagat Arya’ by S.L.Nirmohi. Besides, the post mentions Bhikku Bodhanand as the godfather of the anti-Brahmin thesis in leftist academic circles.

It concludes by saying, “So, if you wonder who created Kanhaiya Kumar or Neha Bora? It is our education system, infested with such books and anti-Hindu propaganda propagated by left-leaning teachers who are also products of the same education system. We need to break this cycle.”

Interestingly, none of these writers mentioned in the post could be characterised as left-leaning. On the contrary, several of them critiqued traditional Indian left from the perspective of caste and gender.

“Ambedkarism was always opposed to the leftist idea of class war. If the PMO stands for opposing Phule, Ambedkar being taught, then it stands against SC/ST/OBCs when the PM himself is an OBC and the President is ST. If the PMO stands for Patriarchy and Manudharma, then it is against man-woman equality,” observed writer and academic Kancha Ilaiah Shepherd, whose three works, including the trailblazing ‘Why I am not a Hindu ’, were listed among the 35 readings attached with the post.

He also questions the interference of the PMO in the syllabus of universities, which ought to be in the purview of the Department of Higher Education or University Grants Commission.

Apart from Mr. Shepherd, the authors whose works were mentioned in the image include E.V. Ramasamy (Periyar), R.S.Sharma, Savitribai Phule, Uma Chakravarti, Suvira Jaiswal, Aloka Parasher, Shireen Ratnagar, G. Aloysius, and Anupama Rao. Their works were cited as prescribed readings for postgraduate and undergraduate studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University, Central University of Punjab, Delhi University, and Asutosh College affiliated to University of Calcutta.

title: The architecture of 2030: why the future of global higher education belongs to co-creation
summary:
After decades of treating cross-border degree delivery as a one-way export, the sector's real growth lies in combining agile delivery with genuine academic co-creation, writes Gaganjot Kaur.

The post The architecture of 2030: why the future of global higher education belongs to co-creation appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
For decades, our sector convinced institutions that an offshore branch campus or direct student recruitment was the gold standard. We built an entire industry around exporting: taking an established Western degree model, wrapping it in strong institutional branding, and placing it in a new geography.

Today, in conversations with university leaders, policy makers and higher education stakeholders from London to Riyadh, the same urgent questions keep surfacing about the future of degree delivery, academic capacity building and national growth.

The UK government’s ambition to grow annual education exports to £40 billion by 2030 creates a significant opportunity for the sector. Realising it will take more than inbound, campus-based recruitment alone; it calls for new, collaborative models of delivering accredited higher education.

At the same time, fast-scaling economies are no longer asking for off-the-shelf overseas degrees; they want in-country capacity built alongside local institutions and industry. In Saudi Arabia under Vision 2030, data from the Saudi Data and AI Authority (SDAIA) shows AI-related job postings grew by 54% annually between 2018 and 2022, while the pool of AI-skilled workers expanded by 51% per year. National bodies are asking how technology and global partnerships can accelerate access to accredited university programmes within their own borders.

Yet the sector’s traditional answer often remains misaligned. Many of us built our careers on an export mindset, studying what worked in established university systems in order to replicate it elsewhere. When a moment demands genuine, ground-level co-creation, we often default to the old playbooks: build a physical campus that takes seven years, or recruit students away. We still gravitate toward familiar metrics: recruitment targets, brand visibility and physical real estate. That is curious. Perhaps it says something about how comfortable we have become with transactional expansion.

Many of us built our careers on an export mindset, studying what worked in established university systems in order to replicate it elsewhere

This could be the moment to stop asking how to export our universities, and start asking how to co-create higher education with the communities we serve. There are already glimpses of what that looks like:

Agile hybrid pathways: San Diego State University‘s GlobalFlex model, delivered through SDSU Global Campus, offers an instructive example. International students complete foundational coursework remotely in their home country before progressing to on-campus study in San Diego, reducing living costs and easing visa-related barriers while maintaining full academic rigour.

Co-created higher education frameworks: Multi-stakeholder partnerships bring together international universities, local delivery specialists and digital learning platforms to align international courseware with national qualification frameworks. The objective is not corporate training, but long-term, accredited higher education pathways at scale, without the need for costly physical infrastructure.

These models mark a fundamental shift from brand export to true co-creation. Technology and flexible academic pathways are no longer secondary options; they are the central engine for delivering accredited university impact.

The expertise our sector brings to international partnerships at conferences and receptions now needs to be applied with far greater agility: not to sell off-the-shelf programmes, but to sit down with regional partners, listen to what their academic systems actually need, and co-create something that lasts.

The case for cross-border university education is as strong as ever, and the work is happening right now, in real time. But with rising capital costs, shifting student flows and ambitious national export targets, treating higher education expansion as a transactional export business has reached its limit. Co-creation is the only path forward.

title: Why financial literacy is now a leadership capability
summary: The post Why financial literacy is now a leadership capability appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
Hannah Fromageau and Prof Elizabeth Gammie ask how often do financial decisions affect your work, even when finance isn’t your area of expertise?

Financial pressures are now a defining feature of higher education, influencing decisions about priorities, resources, investment and sustainability. Yet for many leaders, engaging with financial information can feel outside their expertise. The good news is that effective leadership does not require you to become a finance specialist. But it does require the confidence to understand the wider financial context, ask informed questions and contribute meaningfully to decision-making.

Financial literacy as part of everyday leadership

Our Leading with Financial Literacy workshop, part of a series of Leadership Skills Workshops, has been designed with this challenge in mind. Rather than focusing on technical accounting knowledge, the workshop helps participants develop a practical understanding of the financial concepts, language and information that leaders encounter every day. Through discussion and higher education-focused scenarios, participants will explore how financial insight supports better leadership decisions while remaining aligned with institutional mission and values.

Expertise grounded in higher education

The workshop is led by Professor Elizabeth Gammie, Emeritus Professor at Robert Gordon University and an expert in higher education finance and leadership, alongside Hannah Fromageau, Senior Consultant in Leadership and Management at Advance HE. Together, they combine financial expertise with leadership development experience to help participants build confidence in applying financial insight to leadership practice.

The programme has been developed and is delivered in partnership with BUFDG (British Universities Finance Directors Group), ensuring participants benefit from both leadership and financial expertise grounded in the realities facing higher education today.

Building confidence for better decisions

Whether you’re leading a team, managing a budget, contributing to strategic discussions or preparing for broader leadership responsibilities, this workshop will help you feel more confident engaging in financial conversations, interpreting key information and understanding the implications of financial decisions.

Because in today’s higher education landscape, leaders do not need to be financial experts, but they do need to be financially informed.

Hannah Fromageau is a Senior Consultant in Leadership and Management at Advance HE. Drawing on extensive experience designing and facilitating leadership development programmes, she supports higher education professionals to expand their impact, strengthen their practice and navigate the opportunities and challenges of leadership.

Professor Elizabeth Gammie is Emeritus Professor at Robert Gordon University, a chartered accountant and former Dean of Aberdeen Business School.

title: Why should healthcare educators join the Healthcare Educators NET Conference 2026?
summary: The post Why should healthcare educators join the Healthcare Educators NET Conference 2026? appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
Dr Graham Williamson, a nurse academic at Plymouth University School of Nursing and Midwifery, reflects on why the Healthcare Educators NET Conference 2026 offers a welcoming and valuable space for healthcare educators to share ideas, learn from one another and build connections across professions.

For healthcare educators, the opportunity to come together with colleagues from different professions, disciplines and countries can be a powerful source of learning. The Healthcare Educators NET Conference 2026 will provide that opportunity online this year, before returning as a face-to-face event next year.

Dr Graham Williamson has been involved with the conference for many years, first as a presenter, then as a convener, and now as a member of the organising committee. Drawing on that experience, he describes the conference as both supportive for presenters and valuable for anyone seeking fresh perspectives on healthcare education.

A friendly and supportive space to share ideas

One of the conference’s strengths is the supportive environment it creates for those presenting their work. For Graham, this was particularly important when he was a novice researcher and presenter. Sharing ideas with peers, receiving positive responses and being asked thoughtful questions helped build confidence and opened up new ways of thinking about education practice.

That combination of encouragement and constructive challenge is central to the value of the event. It offers presenters the chance not only to disseminate their work, but to test ideas, make connections and engage with others who are working through similar questions in their own contexts.

“I found it a very accepting conference. The attendees were always very positive and asked lots of questions.”

Learning across professions and disciplines

As an international, multidisciplinary conference, it brings together attendees from across the healthcare professions and this breadth matters. “At a time when healthcare education needs to break down barriers and work across silos for the good of patients,” Graham says, “It will be beneficial to make wider contacts and think about how you can work with other professions.”

Graham reflects that, as a nurse, listening to presentations has “opened up my eyes to people in other professions, trying to make sense of education in theirs.”

What stands out, he says, is how much healthcare educators have in common, even when they approach their work from different professional perspectives.

Building wider connections for better healthcare education

The conference is an opportunity to make wider contacts, explore shared issues and consider how collaboration across professions can strengthen healthcare education. For presenters and participants alike, it offers a chance to learn from different approaches while contributing to a supportive community of practice.

Healthcare educators who attend the conference online in 2026 will be joining an event shaped by collegiality, curiosity and a commitment to learning across boundaries. For Graham, that is what has made the conference valuable over many years – and why he hopes others will take part.

title: Reconnecting Smart Thinkers with Communities in Search of Solutions
summary: by Hamish Coates, Ellen Hazelkorn, Hans De Wit, Tessa DeLaquil, and Angel Calderon This blog is based on the editorial for the latest issue of Policy Reviews in Higher Education Executive Snapshot All around the world, academics struggle to publish … Continue reading →
full_text:
by Hamish Coates, Ellen Hazelkorn, Hans De Wit, Tessa DeLaquil, and Angel Calderon

This blog is based on the editorial for the latest issue of Policy Reviews in Higher Education

Executive Snapshot

All around the world, academics struggle to publish articles, editors grumble about review complexities, and communities raise eyebrows over the quality and relevance of the contributions. Unfortunately, readership and relevance seem to be inversely linked to the growing volume of papers. ‘Publish or perish’ anxieties have been overshadowed by concerns about ‘publishing in peril’ and a fading halo around university research.

These are serious issues for the academy. They are serious for editors, including for ourselves at Policy Reviews in Higher Education. Publication relevance matters professionally, and terms of the real-world of policy in which the journal plays. In our latest editorial we formulated steps towards a solution: Editing academic struggles in the era of robot instrumentalism

We also have clarified imperatives and concrete options to step ahead:

Academic networks and stakeholder communities should re-connect with each other

Journal papers should be connected through seminars, social media and blogs with the communities they are intended to benefit

Open webinars are a natural imperative for connecting the solutions posed in academic papers with the problems which prevail in broader communities e.g. Who will fund us? The drifting dynamics of “who pays for what” in higher education

The Big Lion in the Bush

Around the world students flock to universities in seemingly unprecedented numbers and with great zeal but questions abound regarding value-for-money as a result of rising costs and concerns about learner outcomes and quality. At the turn of century, the ‘world class era’ swept in a suite of mechanisms to define and distinguish excellence.

University rankings and other commercial firms positioned themselves as the arbiters of quality and value. In response, universities acquiesced and strove to distinguish themselves using the proffered metrics to build reputation and status and submit hordes of institutional data to be privatised by growing conglomerates. They compiled bibliometric lists to fluff-up brands and augment their purported reputation among academic communities, policymakers and wider society. Universities began to compel academic staff and doctoral students to publish as many journal papers as possible. This game has contributed to the overproduction of papers, of which many are questionable in terms of quality and relevance.

Creaks and hollowness in this game have grown to spur much angst as higher education providers in major powerhouse countries chase increasingly narrow goals. While hitherto profitable for publishers and rankings/ratings agencies, the situation is hardly sustainable. It has become difficult especially for young scholars who are compelled to publish to secure jobs and livelihoods, let alone to raise a family. The value contribution of this ‘publish or perish’ regime is yielding diminishing returns, especially in an era when computers have started citing themselves. Even more challenging is that among these young scholars, doctoral students are forced to publish articles as a requirement for the degree, and in several cases in replacement of the thesis. Not only does this increase the submission and acceptance challenge for them, but also transfers the responsibility of quality review from the supervisors to the journal editors and reviewers, already overloaded with submissions.

Millions of the world’s researchers now work in middle-income economies where far greater value could be given to highly trained faculty. And many of the world’s doctoral graduates will not pursue careers in academia yet are still required to publish as part of their doctoral programmes.

Making Differences not Just Papers

Clearly, university leaders and researchers must work together to stake out a productive future for publishing research or face growing questions of relevance and mistrust. We contend that journal editors must step up to advocate for and design feasible options which go beyond those we find in place today. To have an impact on policy, the application and benefits of higher education research must be communicated appropriately to the wider community.

In a big lumpy world, we must embrace indeed create more diverse publication settings. Even as the robots flourish and do even better at ‘firing digital packets’ between themselves, there remains the problem of how we can promote the idea that publishing multiples of papers is not an end in itself.

It is time to promulgate institutional reforms which ensure that community service related to the academic functions of teaching and research at local, national, and international scales becomes integral to academic roles, beyond merely a focus on mass, global publication.

It is time to recognise more contextualised roles that brilliant academic talent already take in our communities and stop over-egging publication statistics.

Editors in applied fields of research must prioritise academic contributions which make real-world difference. It is ineffective to sit in offices producing ‘papers’ which sit within server farms chewing up fossil-fuelled energy and go nowhere near education communities, institutions, teachers, researchers, industries, or governments. ‘Open access’ has arguably broadened readership somewhat but has failed to reach key sections of society who live and work beyond the rich-world academy and thus address broader questions about substantive value. Indeed, it is ironic that the ‘impact’ forore operates within a paywall echo-chamber!

Academics need to get into their communities. Eating, sparking dialogue, engaging, advising, arguing and building, and linking with leaders and communities who do education, seem to endure as things that matter. It is understandable that certain countries are launching their own publication platforms.

Researchers need to find ways to better communicate their research to the broader societies they intend to serve and find meaningful ways from within their academic functions to respond to social changes. Words like ‘impact’ and ‘engagement’ have been invoked to retrofit relevance around academic practice, though with limited success. It is time to re-humanise academic life and rejoice in its corporeality.

With around half the humans and universities on the planet, it is coming time for Asia, Africa and Latin America to forge their own paths. Most rating agencies, publishers, journals, editors and reviewers are based in Europe and North America, while researcher and author communities are growing elsewhere, especially in Asia. The global system is not in balance, and with the disharmony compounded by politics and competitive tension, it is unlikely that current arrangements will be sustained in coming years, especially given that research in non-Western regions is sprouting and flourishing.

Bringing Thinking Humans Together

A paper which is good for publication is also good for promotion, and for pontification, and pioneering. As academic publication has grown, researchers have become often dangerously detached from the communities they are constituted to serve. Is it too wild to expect that editors should only publish situated papers which are potentially going to have a genuine impact on communities? No, this is not crazy thinking. It is post-digital thinking that reclaims community and collegial purpose in ways which even global tech leaders have started to advocate.

Obviously, there are infinite ways to re-kindle connections between academics and communities. Online webinars are a great way to begin. In 2026 Policy Reviews in Higher Education launched an online global series of webinars. Lamenting the lack of dialogue between policy researchers and policymakers, the journal editors had previously forged links between published papers and blogs and social media.

The webinars shift outreach and engagement to the next level. While modest in terms of contemporary social media ecosystems, such efforts are reasonably venturesome for journals which have grown beyond their initial scholar community and into a global and very much larger world. ‘Global’ has a great ring to it but also implies simultaneously ‘everything to everyone’ and ‘nothing to no-one’. Webinars restore human connection, moving papers and ideas and intellectual advocacy beyond server farms back into real professional, institutional and social lives.

The very first webinar focused on ‘Striving for recognition: University manoeuvres for societal outcomes’. As nations have called for universities to serve different communities, institutions have sought different ways to succeed. Desideria Cempaka Wijaya Murti contributed from Indonesia, Michael Fung and Sabur Butt from Mexico, and Michael Shattock from the United Kingdom. The three policy pitches provided perspectives from their respective countries / regions and highlighted emerging research trends and present thought-provoking ideas to help shape future policy directions.

Webinar number two focused on a hot topic of our times: ‘Transnational education (TNE) in the wild: Quality shocks, international anarchy, and academic disconnection. The three policy pitches approached this phenomenon from distinct yet complementary perspectives. Jason E. Lane (United States) talked about geopolitical infrastructure, Lilan Chen (Japan) provided compelling insights into student-centred quality and access, and Jeanette Baird (Australia, Papua New Guinea) gave expert insights into tertiary regulation and risk governance. Together, the discussion highlighted the growing complexity of TNE and the need to better understand its implications for students, institutions, governments, and societies.

The third webinar focuses on money, pricing, transparency, and value. It is titled: ‘Who will fund us? The drifting dynamics of “who pays for what” in higher education’. This webinar will explore questions around who pays and what kind of service to expect and need into the future. The policy pitches will be made by Christopher Millward (United Kingdom), N.V. Varghese (India), Lorraine Dearden (United Kingdom) and Huw Morris (United Kingdom). Almost everything which is known about higher education funding refers to rich countries. With major growth now erupting in Africa, ASEAN and Eurasia, it is time to build evidence and dialogue into other situations and growth options.

We are lucky to work as professionals across the fantastic and expanding tertiary landscape. Now is a time for us to work together to co-create new futures. We have no time to wring our hands and give up higher thinking to commercial raters. We cannot afford to let computer scientists and accountants alone define all the futures. These professionals are part of our broader academic and professional community. They need our help as much as we need theirs. The challenges and opportunities before us are great. We need all experts to work together.

Hamish Coates is a global leader in higher education with major contributions to policy and innovation who designs and strengthens higher education systems, institutions and leadership.

Ellen Hazelkorn is Joint Managing Partner, BH Associates education consultants, and Professor Emeritus, Technological University Dublin (Ireland).

Hans de Wit is Professor Emeritus of the Practice and Distinguished Fellow and Former Director (2015-2020) of the Center for International Higher Education, Boston College, USA.

Tessa DeLaquil is Associate Professor at the Department for Pedagogy and Lifelong Learning at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

Angel Calderon is director, strategic insights, at RMIT University, Melbourne, Australia.

The Power of Sisterhood

September 28, 2026, by Dean Hoke: Over the years, I have spoken with many small college leaders searching for a clearer sense of what distinguishes their institutions. Some have developed new academic programs, expanded athletics, or reconsidered traditional missions to attract students. Spelman College offers a different perspective, having built its national reputation around an identity that has remained remarkably consistent since its founding in 1881.

Located in Atlanta, Spelman is a historically Black liberal arts college dedicated to the education of women. It enrolls approximately 2,600 undergraduates, attracts more than 11,000 applications for its entering class, and retains approximately 95 percent of first-year students. Its reputation extends well beyond the HBCU community, but those measures tell only part of the story.

Central to understanding Spelman is the Sisterhood, a connection that begins when students arrive and continues long after graduation. Through traditions, faculty relationships, mentoring, and an alumnae community of more than 21,000 women, the College has developed a culture in which the student–institution relationship is intended to last a lifetime. Graduates contribute professional networks, leadership, and a continuing sense of belonging.

For small colleges confronting questions about enrollment and identity, Spelman offers a useful example. Rather than redefining its mission to appeal to a broader market, it has built upon the purpose established by its founders 145 years ago. Sometimes a college’s greatest strength lies in understanding what has made it distinctive all along.

The Origins of Spelman College

Spelman’s history begins in the years following the Civil War, when educational opportunities for Black women in the South were severely limited. On April 11, 1881, Sophia B. Packard and Harriet E. Giles opened the Atlanta Baptist Female Seminary in the basement of Friendship Baptist Church. With just 11 students and $100, they established an institution dedicated to providing Black women and girls with educational opportunities largely denied to them.

Financial support from John D. Rockefeller helped the school expand and acquire property. In 1883, it moved to its present site; in 1884 it was renamed Spelman Seminary for Laura Spelman Rockefeller and her parents, Harvey Buel and Lucy Henry Spelman, who had been active in the antislavery movement. It became Spelman College in 1924.

From its earliest years, Spelman combined liberal education with professional preparation. Teacher education developed early, nursing instruction began in 1886, and the college awarded its first degrees in 1901. Those milestones are worth remembering because the founders did more than open another school. They were creating opportunities for Black women to enter professions, support their families, and exercise influence in communities where such opportunities had long been restricted.

That purpose remains evident 145 years later. Spelman has expanded into science and technology while retaining its commitment to preparing Black women for leadership and professional achievement.

A Small College with Considerable Demand

Spelman’s enrollment experience differs from that of many small private colleges. For the Class of 2029, entering in fall 2025, the College received more than 11,500 first-year applications, admitted fewer than one-quarter of applicants, and enrolled approximately 650 new students. The entering class represented 37 states and U.S. territories and three foreign countries, with only about 22 percent coming from Georgia.

Spelman’s appeal is national rather than primarily regional. While many small colleges depend upon nearby populations, its mission, reputation, and alumnae network attract students from well beyond Atlanta.

Enrollment Trend

Spelman enrolled 2,125 undergraduates in fall 2016 and 2,597 in fall 2025, an increase of approximately 22.2 percent. Growth was not perfectly linear: enrollment reached 2,417 in 2021, slipped to 2,374 the following year, and then rose to 2,712 in 2024 before declining to 2,597 in 2025. A one-year decline warrants attention, but it does not erase the larger pattern. Over the decade, Spelman added nearly 500 students while continuing to receive many more applications than it could accommodate.

Spelman and the Changing Landscape of Women’s Colleges

In the mid-20th century, more than 200 women’s colleges existed in the United States. By fall 2022, 31 remained. Some institutions closed or merged, while others became coeducational in response to changing student preferences, enrollment pressures, and financial circumstances.

Enrollment across the sector has also contracted. Between 1998 and 2022, total enrollment at women’s colleges declined 40 percent, from approximately 112,500 students to 67,300. The decline was 18 percent during the final decade of that period alone. Spelman’s documented fall enrollment increased between 2020 and 2024, although this shorter period should not be treated as directly comparable with the sector-wide 1998–2022 trend.

Spelman is one of only two remaining women’s colleges that are also historically Black colleges, the other being Bennett College in North Carolina. Nevertheless, some of its useful academic peers are institutions such as Wellesley, Smith, Mount Holyoke, Bryn Mawr, and Scripps. These colleges share longstanding commitments to undergraduate liberal arts education, selective admissions, and influential alumnae communities, although their histories, student populations, and financial resources differ considerably.

Spelman has not responded to the contraction of women’s colleges by abandoning its identity. Its experience suggests that a specialized mission need not limit demand when students understand the community and education it offers.

Student Success Beyond Admission

Application numbers tell only part of the story. Spelman’s second-year retention rate is approximately 95 percent, and its six-year graduation rate has generally remained in the mid-to-upper 70s in recent cohorts.

For students who entered in 2018, Spelman reported a six-year graduation rate of 78 percent, compared with 58 percent nationally and 39 percent among four-year HBCUs. That result substantially exceeded the four-year HBCU average, although several of its selective women’s-college peers report higher rates.

Those outcomes reflect a strong record of student persistence, although important differences remain. For the 2019 entering cohort, the six-year graduation rate for Pell Grant recipients was 67 percent, below the rate for students who did not receive Pell Grants. Affordability is therefore a question of degree completion as well as admission.

STEM Within a Liberal Arts Education

One of the more interesting aspects of Spelman is its record in science and technology. The College is not a technical institute, nor does it operate an engineering or medical school. Its mission instead describes an institution dedicated to “academic excellence in the liberal arts and sciences and the intellectual, creative, ethical, and leadership development of its students.” It also emphasizes educating the whole person, while its formal Statement of Purpose encompasses the fine arts, humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences.

Spelman reports that, over a five-year period described on its STEM webpage, an average of 34 percent of students pursued STEM majors and approximately one-quarter of graduates earned STEM degrees. The webpage does not specify the reporting years.

Spelman has developed STEM strength without replacing its liberal arts environment. Students preparing for scientific careers also study writing, communication, and disciplines concerned with human behavior, culture, and ethics. It reflects the College’s longstanding expectation that a graduate should be able to bring several ways of thinking to bear on a problem, whether she is working in a laboratory, a classroom, a business, or public life.

That breadth may become increasingly important as artificial intelligence changes professional work. AI can already assist with tasks in software development, research, and analysis, but technical expertise remains essential. What may become more distinctive is the ability to apply that expertise with judgment.

Scientists and engineers who assume broader responsibilities must decide which problems deserve attention, assess incomplete information, communicate across specialties, and understand the human consequences of their work. Creativity, ethical reasoning, and leadership complement rather than replace technical skills.

A Spelman student may become a biologist, mathematician, or computer scientist while also studying history, philosophy, literature, and the arts. That breadth does not guarantee professional success, but it may help graduates adapt as technologies and occupations change.

Spelman’s current institutional priorities suggest that the College recognizes this opportunity. Its Spelman Forward campaign calls for integrating AI literacy, computational reasoning, and ethical leadership across the curriculum while modernizing its liberal arts foundation. The emphasis is not on replacing the liberal arts with technology, but on preparing students to understand and use technology within a broader intellectual and human context.

The Faculty and Research Behind the Results

Spelman’s STEM accomplishments also depend upon faculty and research opportunities. The College reports 54 full-time faculty members in its STEM departments and programs, 83 percent of whom are members of racial or ethnic minority groups and 52 percent of whom are women. Nearly two-thirds of the women on its STEM faculty are African American.

Students can work with faculty engaged in research rather than encounter science only in the classroom. In a smaller undergraduate setting, the relationship between a professor and a student can extend from introductory coursework to laboratory work, mentoring, and conversations about graduate study. Spelman also participates in externally supported research and undergraduate research programs.

Spelman has also attracted federal research support, including participation in grants that expand research opportunities for its students and faculty. In 2024, it led an Atlanta University Center consortium awarded $14 million through the National Science Foundation’s GRANTED program, an initiative intended to strengthen research infrastructure and competitiveness at participating HBCUs. The award was made to the consortium, not to Spelman alone, but it illustrates how the College uses collaboration to expand what its faculty and students can undertake.

Faculty, external support, and partnerships extend research opportunities beyond Spelman’s own campus.

An Engineering Program Built Through Partnership

Spelman’s approach to engineering offers another example of expanding educational opportunities without attempting to become a larger institution. Through the Atlanta University Center’s Dual Degree Engineering Program, students generally complete at least three years at Spelman and two years at a partner engineering institution. Those who satisfy both institutions’ requirements receive a bachelor’s degree from Spelman and an engineering degree from the partner.

The program includes 15 engineering partners, among them Georgia Tech, Columbia University, Purdue University, and the University of Michigan. Students can therefore begin their undergraduate education within Spelman’s liberal arts environment and complete specialized engineering study at institutions with established programs and facilities.

The arrangement illustrates a practical distinction between the size of an institution and the range of opportunities available to its students. An engineering school requires specialized faculty, laboratories, equipment, and continuing investment. By working with established partners, Spelman can preserve its own undergraduate educational model while offering students a route into a field that would otherwise require resources beyond its campus.

The Spelman Sisterhood

The College’s academic record explains only part of its influence. Spelman’s alumnae community, which the institution reports numbers 21,785 women, has become another important source of professional opportunity, philanthropy, and institutional continuity.

Its graduates include Marian Wright Edelman, Class of 1960, founder of the Children’s Defense Fund; Audrey Forbes Manley, Class of 1955, a physician and former Acting Surgeon General who later became Spelman’s first alumna president; and Rosalind Brewer, Class of 1984, whose corporate leadership career included serving as CEO of Walgreens Boots Alliance. Brewer subsequently returned to Spelman as a trustee leader and interim president.

Other graduates include economist Lisa D. Cook, Class of 1986, who became a member of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, and Evelynn Hammonds, Class of 1976, a historian of science and medicine who served as Dean of Harvard College. Their careers span public service, medicine, business, economics, and higher education, reflecting the breadth of opportunities Spelman graduates pursue.

The alumnae network extends beyond prominent names. Graduates mentor students, provide professional contacts, contribute financially, and help lead the College, connecting current students with women who followed similar paths. The presence of alumnae in campus life gives undergraduates examples of what a Spelman education can lead to, while shared traditions encourage graduates to see themselves as continuing participants in the College’s story rather than former customers of an educational institution.

Rosalind Brewer’s return as interim president offers a particularly tangible example. When Spelman needed leadership during a presidential transition, it turned to a graduate who understood the institution and had accumulated extensive experience elsewhere. The Sisterhood, in that instance, became more than a tradition or professional network; it became an institutional resource.

Beyond the Brochure

One of Spelman’s most recognizable traditions is wearing white. Dating to around 1900, the practice began when students were expected to have a conservative white dress for formal occasions. Spelman describes the tradition as creating a uniform appearance and marking the importance of formal occasions.

The tradition has endured for more than a century. First-year students wear white during their induction into the Spelman Sisterhood, while white attire also appears at Founders Day and major commencement-related events. Alumnae returning for Reunion participate in the March Through the Alumnae Arch, maintaining a connection with customs observed by generations before them. Students encounter its history in ways that are visible, shared, and repeated across generations.

These traditions make the idea of Sisterhood tangible.

Atlanta and the Atlanta University Center

Spelman’s location provides educational opportunities that would be difficult to duplicate in a more isolated setting. The College belongs to the Atlanta University Center, a consortium of historically Black institutions that includes Morehouse College and Clark Atlanta University. Cross-registration and institutional cooperation expand the academic and social opportunities available to students while allowing Spelman to maintain its own identity and relatively small enrollment.

Atlanta itself offers access to major corporations, health systems, cultural institutions, research organizations, and an extensive Black professional community. The city’s history also provides an important educational context. Spelman students participated in the Atlanta Student Movement during the 1960s, linking the College to the broader struggle for civil rights and the development of the city.

Students thus experience a small college within a much larger educational and metropolitan community.

Financial Strength and the Challenge of Access

Spelman possesses financial resources that distinguish it from many small private colleges. At June 30, 2025, it reported more than $1 billion in total assets, approximately $964 million in net assets, and an endowment of roughly $609 million. According to the Hechinger Report’s Financial Fitness Tracker, net tuition represented 19 percent of its 2024 revenue, versus a 45 percent median among private nonprofit colleges. That lower dependence on tuition provides context for assessing its financial position.

Financial Trends

Spelman’s operating revenue increased substantially between FY2021 and FY2024 before declining in FY2025. Operating expenses also rose over the five-year period, narrowing the positive operating margin considerably in FY2025.

Restricted gifts, endowment activity, and capital projects can affect annual results, so a single year should not be mistaken for a sustained trend.

Spelman’s recent fundraising has been substantial. In January 2024, trustee Ronda Stryker and her husband, William Johnston, announced a $100 million gift, including $75 million for endowed scholarships. MacKenzie Scott contributed $38 million in unrestricted support in 2025, following a $20 million gift in 2020. The Arthur M. Blank Family Foundation has also committed $16.5 million over ten years to support scholarships for Spelman juniors and seniors with significant financial need.

Among Spelman’s 2024 graduates, 62 percent borrowed, with average cumulative student debt of $34,425 among borrowers. For 2023–24 graduates of private nonprofit four-year institutions nationally, the College Board reports an almost identical average of $34,420 among borrowers, but only 49 percent of graduates borrowed.

In April 2026, Spelman launched its $500 million *Spelman Forward* campaign. Approximately $325 million—65 percent—is designated for access and affordability, with another $100 million for academic transformation, including AI literacy and ethical leadership.

Despite strong demand and philanthropy, affordability remains central to Spelman’s strategy, alongside investment in a liberal arts curriculum suited to technological change.

A New President and the Next Chapter

Spelman enters this period of academic and financial investment under new leadership. Mary Schmidt Campbell served as president from 2015 until her retirement in 2022. Her successor, Helene Gayle, left the presidency in 2024, after which Rosalind Brewer served as interim president. Brewer’s appointment brought an experienced corporate leader and Spelman graduate back to the institution during an important transition.

On August 1, 2026, Ayanna Howard became Spelman’s 12th president. A roboticist and artificial intelligence researcher, Howard previously worked at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, held a faculty position at Georgia Tech, co-founded the robotics company Zyrobotics, and served as dean of the College of Engineering at Ohio State University.

Howard inherits established STEM programs, research partnerships, and an ambition to integrate AI literacy into a liberal arts education; she is not creating a scientific identity from scratch.

It is too early to evaluate her presidency, but her background makes the relationship between scientific education and Spelman’s broader mission especially interesting. Her appointment brings the story back to a question that has shaped Spelman since its founding: how to prepare women for emerging opportunities without losing the educational purpose that distinguishes the College.

Why Is Spelman College Important?

Spelman’s experience offers several lessons for small private colleges, particularly those confronting questions about enrollment, academic identity, financial resources, and the future of liberal arts education.

Distinctiveness Is More Powerful When It Is Authentic. Spelman’s mission has remained remarkably consistent while the number of women’s colleges has declined dramatically. Its history, academic programs, student experience, and alumnae community reinforce an identity that prospective students can readily understand. The College’s experience suggests that differentiation is most effective when it reflects an institution’s actual educational purpose rather than a marketing response to changing circumstances.

Liberal Arts and STEM Can Strengthen One Another. Spelman demonstrates that a small liberal arts college can prepare substantial numbers of students for scientific careers without abandoning a broader education. As artificial intelligence changes professional work, the combination of technical knowledge with communication, creativity, ethical reasoning, adaptability, and leadership may become increasingly valuable. Spelman’s commitment to bringing AI literacy into its liberal arts curriculum makes this an especially relevant part of its story.

Partnership Can Substitute for Scale. The dual-degree engineering program, Atlanta University Center, and external research relationships allow Spelman to offer educational opportunities that would be difficult to provide entirely on its own. These arrangements suggest that a small institution need not become a comprehensive university to give students access to specialized fields and facilities.

Alumnae Can Be Part of the Educational Model. The Sisterhood extends the relationship between student and institution beyond graduation. Through mentoring, professional connections, philanthropy, and leadership, alumnae contribute to the experience of current students and the continuing development of the College. Rosalind Brewer’s service as interim president demonstrates how those connections can become particularly valuable during institutional transitions.

Financial Strength Creates Choices, Not Immunity. Spelman’s assets, endowment, and recent philanthropic support give it options that many small colleges do not possess. Yet its decision to direct nearly two-thirds of a $500 million campaign toward access and affordability shows that financial resources must still align with students’ needs and the institution’s mission.

What makes Spelman interesting is the coherence of its mission, academic programs, traditions, and alumnae relationships.

A student can enter the Sisterhood, study across disciplines, conduct research, and pursue engineering through a partner institution. Along the way, she encounters an academic community that expects both professional preparation and broader intellectual development. At graduation, she passes through the Alumnae Arch into a network that may shape her life for decades.

The college that began with 11 students in an Atlanta church basement remains relatively small 145 years later, but its influence reaches far beyond campus.

Additional sources: Spelman College, 2025–26 Common Data Set, Section H5 (student debt); FY26 Student Achievement Report (Pell graduation); The Hechinger Report, Financial Fitness Tracker (2024 net-tuition share); College Board, Trends in College Pricing and Student Aid 2025, Figure SA-14A (national debt comparison).

Dean Hoke is Executive Producer and co-host of Small College America and Managing Partner of Edu Alliance Group, a higher education consulting firm based in Bloomington, Indiana, and Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. He formerly served as President/CEO of the American Association of University Administrators (AAUA) and has worked with colleges and universities in the United States and internationally throughout his career.

title: Why the latest action from India's youth-led 'cockroach' movement is targeting the election chief
summary: The 'cockroach' movement has emerged as an influential force in Indian politics. Its latest campaign targets the election commission amid a wider debate over voter rolls and public trust in electoral institutions.
full_text:
India's youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and opposition parties have demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar after a newspaper investigation alleged impropriety during a large-scale voter-roll revision.

According to the probe, published in The Indian Express newspaper, some key decisions linked to the so-called Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls that began last year were likely taken without the approval of two of the three election commissioners.

The Indian Express said that fellow Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months to decisions concerning voter registrations, deletions and restorations, as well as control of electoral-roll data.

In one of the objections, Sandhu complained that the Election Commission of India (ECI) acted against the written advice of two commissioners and claimed its action was "unauthorized and illegal."

The allegations presented "only one part of the picture," and "differing views" were a routine "part of decision-making," the ECI said in a statement cited by local media.

'Cockroach' movement founder calls for demonstrations

Speaking at a press conference on Thursday, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke called Kumar "the biggest threat to India's democracy" and demanded his resignation.

Dipke threatened to launch nationwide protests, beginning in Mumbai on October 2, the birthday of India's founding father Mahatma Gandhi, if Kumar did not quit by Saturday.

The Saturday deadline passed without Kumar stepping down.

After Mumbai police denied permission for the planned October 2 protest, Dipke posted on X calling on supporters to submit to mass arrests rather than comply with the ban.

Supporters staged protests on Friday and pledged to continue mobilizing despite the restrictions.

Opposition parties echoed the CJP's criticism of Kumar and the Election Commission.

Pawan Khera of the main opposition Congress party said that "Gyanesh Kumar has done nothing short of treason."

"If decisions relating to the SIR were taken without the knowledge or approval of two of the three election commissioners... then those decisions and the entire SIR exercise are legally invalid," Khera said on social media.

Congress and other opposition parties have accused the ECI of colluding with India's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) to manipulate voter lists and win state elections in recent years, charges both the commission and the BJP have denied.

What are the demands of India's CJP movement?

The 'Cockroach' movement, which has millions of followers on social media, forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign in July following widespread student-led street protests.

The group has laid out three demands: Kumar's resignation and criminal proceedings against him, a freeze on the SIR and the suspension of all upcoming elections, and the repeal of the 2023 law on the appointment of the election commissioners of India.

Civil rights activist Amrita Johri said the CJP's decision to target the poll panel reflects wider concerns over the lack of transparency surrounding the SIR.

"There is an absence of public consultation or a clear explanation for launching the exercise, as well as the findings of the newspaper that the two election commissioners had raised repeated objections to key decisions," Johri told DW.

"Restoring public confidence will require Kumar's removal, stopping the SIR and an independent review of the millions of names excluded from the draft rolls."

From education protests to electoral politics

Political activist Sudheendra Kulkarni sees the CJP's latest campaign as that of a pressure group rather than an emerging standalone political force.

"I do not see any separate political future for the CJP. It may remain as a pressure group for some time. But as the next parliamentary election approaches, it will have to align itself with the opposition alliance," Kulkarni told DW.

Others see greater weight in the CJP's shift.

Political analyst and commentator Radhika Ramaseshan said the CJP widening its focus will not weaken what it started.

"I don't think if the CJP enlarged the ambit of its concerns and built protests around [them], it would take away from the salience and power of the first issue it highlighted," Ramaseshan told DW. "Voter rights and enfranchisement is fundamental to a citizen's existence, to upholding the sanctity of the Indian constitution."

"These are not abstractions or procedural matters. They impinge on the lives of first-time voters who make up the bulk of the CJP," she added.

What happens now?

With Kumar refusing to resign, attention will now turn to the CJP's promise of street protests starting in Mumbai on October 2.

But a protest group alone cannot simply remove a CEC. Under India's constitution, the CEC can be removed only through a process requiring action by both houses of Parliament and a special majority, on grounds of proved misbehavior or incapacity.

"The CJP's significance would be in increasing pressure and forcing scrutiny of the ECI's functioning," former Chief Election Commissioner S Y Quraishi's told DW.

He argues that the reported unilateral decisions are the more serious issue and should be subjected to an independent legal and technical audit.

"The practical route is judicial scrutiny, not street removal. The decisions taken unilaterally by the CEC in a three-member commission could be challenged as invalid, with the Supreme Court potentially needed to intervene," he said.

"Where the commission will not act, the Supreme Court will have to step in," added Quraishi.

The CJP's latest campaign puts it directly into one of India's most contentious disputes over electoral administration.

Whether it can sustain that momentum against the Election Commission will be a very different test for a movement that is still trying to define its place in Indian politics.

title: Digitale Gewalt im Netz: Mehrheit der Frauen schränkt Verhalten im Internet ein
summary: Aus Angst vor digitaler Gewalt verändern zwei Drittel der Frauen ihr Verhalten im Internet, besonders betroffen sind junge Frauen. Das zeigt eine Umfrage.
full_text:

Aus Angst vor digitaler und KI-gestützter sexualisierter Gewalt schränken immer mehr Frauen ihr Verhalten in digitalen Räumen und ziehen sich vorsorglich zurück. Das ist der zentrale Befund einer repräsentativen Umfrage, deren Ergebnis der Deutsche Frauenrat am Montag veröffentlicht hat. Besonders betroffen sind demnach junge Frauen, jede fünfte im Alter zwischen 18 und 39 Jahren war demnach bereits mit sexualisierten Deepfake-Bildern von sich konfrontiert. Knapp ein Drittel habe erleben müssen, dass intime Bilder ohne Einwilligung verbreitet wurden, mehr als jeder achten Frau sei online sexualisierte Gewalt angedroht worden. Der Interessenverband fordert die Politik deshalb zum Handeln auf und untermauert die Warnung mit erschreckenden Stellungnahmen.

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Forderungen an die Politik

Der Deutsche Frauenrat setzt sich als Dachverband von über 60 Verbänden für frauenpolitische Interessen ein und hat für die Analyse jetzt 1380 Frauen vom Bilendi Institut befragen lassen. Die Ergebnisse passen demnach zu den bisherigen Erkenntnissen über digitale Gewalt „und zeigen zugleich eine neue Dimension des Problems“. Die Antworten machen deutlich, „dass digitale Gewalt nicht nur die unmittelbar Betroffenen trifft“. Sie verändere das Verhalten einer Mehrheit der Frauen, schränke ihre Sichtbarkeit und Teilhabe online ein und wirke weit über einzelne Übergriffe hinaus. Daraus ergebe sich ein klarer politischer Handlungsauftrag, die Befragten erwarteten einen wirksamen Schutz, der über das geplante „Digitale Gewalt“-Gesetz hinausgehe. 92 Prozent fordern etwa eine Bestrafung der Verbreitung sexualisierter Deepfakes, 91 Prozent eine Bestrafung ihrer Herstellung

Laut der Zusammenfassung der Umfrageergebnisse haben fast 90 Prozent der Befragten der Aussage, „Ich vermeide es, Bilder/Videos/Informationen zu posten“ komplett oder teilweise zugestimmt. Bei „Ich verzichte bewusst auf Online-Aktivitäten“ waren es weit über 80 Prozent. Besonders stark ist der Rückzug demnach bei Frauen, die schon einmal digitale oder digital-sexualisierte Gewalt erlebt haben, aber sogar 57 Prozent der Befragten ohne diesen Hintergrund würden sich einschränken. Das zeige, dass die Angst vor digitaler Gewalt auch ohne eigene Betroffenheit für Verhaltensänderung sorge. Digitale Gewalt zwinge Frauen also „zu präventiver Selbstbeschränkung: weniger Sichtbarkeit, weniger Austausch, weniger Teilhabe“.

In dem Bericht heißt es weiter, dass fast die Hälfte der Befragten bereits mindestens einmal online unerwünschte sexualisierte Nachrichten, Kommentare oder Aufforderungen erhalten habe. Jede dritte Frau habe solche Erfahrungen sogar gelegentlich, mehrfach oder häufig gemacht. Von direkt Betroffenen haben demnach zudem 44 Prozent angegeben, dass unerlaubt verbreitete Inhalte teilweise oder gar nicht gelöscht wurden, bei weiteren 20 Prozent war der Status der Entfernung aus dem Internet unklar. Um die Folgen digitaler Gewalt deutlich zu machen, wurden in dem Bericht auch mehrere anonyme Erfahrungsberichte abgedruckt:

„Mir wurde durch einen Mitschüler meines Sohnes angedroht, dass er mich vergewaltigen will.“

„Männer haben mir geschrieben, dass wenn sie mich finden, mich in der Gruppe vergewaltigen und die Videos dann im Internet teilen.“

„Ein anderer Mann hat mich zum Sex erpressen wollen und Pornovideos mit meinem Gesicht erstellt und Nacktbilder und auf Facebook an meine Freunde geschickt. Die Polizei hat mir gesagt, dass ich da nichts machen kann, außer auf meiner Facebook Seite schreiben, dass ich NICHT die Person auf dem Bild bin.... aber es war mein Gesicht und damit sehr demütigend.“

„Mein Ex hat gedroht, Bilder ins Internet zu stellen, wenn ich ihn verlasse. Irgendein Fremder hat in einem Chat, nachdem ich das Gespräch beenden wollte, gedroht, wenn er rausbekommt, wo ich mich rumtreibe, würde er mich eines Tages vergewaltigen.“
